I made a comment on a thread a day or so ago about Homefront, a shooter from 2011, and it got some good response, so I thought I'd elaborate on my thoughts a bit and give it a fair review. This review doesn't 'follow on' exactly, but I mention a couple notes there I don't mention here. Still though - the review:

I - really - liked Homefront. Something about the game I just really, really loved. The majority of gamers called it shit, as did the critics, and Homefront virtually disappeared into obscurity. Dubbed in the early impressions at E3 etc, it was to be the 'Half-Life killer', or something along those lines, as it featured a similar storyline of a nation under siege and the formation of the Resistance to repel the invaders. That said however, it didn't quite live up to the name.

The storyline is probably the most outlandish thing in the whole game. Homefront opens up with a FMV-style timeline of events, showing an alternate history that parallels today's, and a way that the world could've gone. That, in short, is North and South Korea re-uniting, forming the 'Greater Korean Republic' (utilising the economic strength of the South and military power of the North), becoming a superpower, and eventually kickstarts Homefront with the invasion of the United States. As I said, it's outlandish and pretty unrealistic. But I think that, personally, this is what Homefront takes in it's stride. If anything, it's more of an action movie with a couple 'out there' setpieces and events than a realistic war story, but as a more subtle reminder that war can happen anywhere, which I feel drives home the message, and game's tagline, that 'home is where the war is', given we all have our own problems and whatnot.

To bring it back to the game, I myself quite enjoyed the plot. The campaign is noticeably short, and could easily be clocked within a day, but I don't think that any of the levels are dragged out as such - more short, sweet, and to the point. However, the opening cutscene after the initial timeline clip is fairly brutal, quite hard hitting, and actually one of the best that I've ever seen in games for the last few years. The campaign also has a couple scenes that are fairly graphic, vivid, and could be considered quite disturbing. I guess I 'enjoyed' them? I mean, it's not everyday you play a game that attempts to pull it off, but I guess it's more to consider that Homefront isn't as generic a shooter as you might think. The characters aren't particularly fleshed out, but you, as the character, join the Resistance later in terms of the overall plot, so it's unlikely you'd have met them when shit first hit the fan anyway. As such, the game does quite a good job of making you 'feel' like an outsider - as I said in the post I made, you're more of a 'small cog in a larger machine' than a 'one man army', which I really, really enjoy, although the bodies of all the enemies you've killed might beg to differ. It is a first-person shooter, after all.

Then we come to the core gameplay, and, unsurprisingly, it's generally stale. Homefront doesn't do anything to reinvent the wheel in the FPS genre, although I wouldn't say it needed to, given the formula is proven well time and time again for recognized franchises like Call of Duty, so I see why they might've had the mindset of 'don't fix what's not broken', but I think it was more of a gamble for one with an unproven track record given it's such a new IP, and ultimately one that didn't pay off. There's some variety in the guns on offer, albeit limited, but ironically, the game's short enough to feel that you're not using the same one all the way through. A couple of levels also provide some, as others might say, much needed variety, but I'm more inclined to feel that's it's more to break up the slog of constant shooting galleries the game provides - and one the game deserves; they're fairly entertaining for what it's worth, and the "Goliath mechanic" (an unmanned, armoured, remote control ground vehicle) occasionally shows up to remind the player the resistance won't take any shit. You could call them gimmicks, but I think it adds to the 'action movie vibe' the game has all the way through.

The multiplayer, however, is where Homefront really excels, or 'once excelled' if you're after accuracy. The multiplayer featured a couple of modes, but operated on a 'points system'. Points were available by killing enemies, destroying enemy vehicles, ending enemy player's killstreaks, destroying enemy drones, capturing command posts, etc, etc. With these points, you could bring in different special equipment, like drones, airstrikes, or vehicles like tanks and helicopters. What was good about this system was that the players who were good were rewarded as such, rather than a system like Battlefield, where you wait for the vehicle to spawn and jump at the chance. Games could be fairly long as well, meaning that if the game was 1-1 after 2/3 round in Ground Control (pushing the enemy further back along a bigger map), the final firefight was very shooty-shooty-bang-bang, with mashing buttons to get back in the fight as soon as possible. Unfortunately, what with the GameSpy shutdown, Homefront's multiplayer on the PS3 and 360 is now at an end, but a couple of dedicated servers still remain on the PC. That said, it's quiet for the most part, and I look back at Homefront's multiplayer with fond memories of days gone by.

I could ramble on about how I don't think it didn't get the attention it deserved, which I do think was true, but also inadvertently almost entirely it's own fault. It didn't leave a very good first impression, and I approach Homefront: The Revolution, a sequel coming next year, with some caution, given I actually enjoyed the original. Still, we'll have to wait and see.

4/10: I personally enjoyed the story, although short, and the now-dead multiplayer was Homefront's main redeeming factor back in the day. The graphics aren't great, the story is unrealistic, but more modern day shooters, I feel, need to look back at Homefront and push the boundaries in the now-saturated genre of first person shooters. Homefront struck a bit of a chord with me, and it's an experience I at least can look back and remember fondly.
